name: Dynamic versus static pleasure
plain_explanation: Epicurus distinguished the pleasure of actively satisfying a craving (like the enjoyment of eating when hungry) from the calmer pleasure of simply not being troubled by any craving at all (the quiet state after hunger is satisfied). He judged the second, calmer kind of pleasure better and safer to pursue.
precise_definition: 'Dynamic' (or active) pleasures are those attained through the process of satisfying a prior desire that was accompanied by pain; 'static' pleasures consist in a state of painless equilibrium that results simply from the absence of unsatisfied desire, requiring no painful stimulus beforehand.
why_it_mattered: This distinction leads Epicurus to redefine the wise life's goal as absence of pain (aponia) and freedom from disturbance (ataraxia) rather than the pursuit of intense pleasurable experiences, making his 'hedonism' far more austere in practice than the word suggests.
historical_origin: Epicurus's own refinement of earlier hedonist doctrine (e.g. of the Cyrenaics, though not named in this chapter), distinguishing his position from theirs.
examples: Epicurus living contentedly on bread and water, calling this itself a thrilling bodily pleasure
His preference to be always in the state of 'having eaten moderately' rather than 'in that of voracious desire to eat'
